```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
ffmpeg_ok <- !inherits(try(AudiomothR:::ffmpeg_path(), silent = TRUE), "try-error")
```

This document goes through the whole workflow of **AudiomothR** with an
example card included in the package: from reading `CONFIG.TXT` and taking
the inventory of the recordings to creating an example (audio, spectrogram
and video), **validating the records by ear** and exporting a CSV file for
Observation.org.

```
AudioMoth card ─► read_audiomoth()  (with copy_to: copy of the card on the disk)
   ─► prepare_audio() ─► analyze_birdnet()  (location filter or own species list)
   ─► species_summary() / detected_species() ─► extract_examples()
   ─► create_validation()  (optional: check the records by ear)
   ─► export_observation() ─► create_report()  (optional: PDF report)
```

**BirdNET needs Python and, the first time, downloading its model from the
Internet**, so this vignette does not run `analyze_birdnet()`: it shows how to
use it and, for the following steps, loads the **real** detections obtained
when the example card was analysed with `analyze_birdnet()` (BirdNET v2.4,
default options), which are included in the package.

## The example data

The package includes, in `inst/extdata/example/card/`, an AudioMoth card: a
`CONFIG.TXT` file and two daily folders (`20261007/` and `20261015/`) with 8
recordings each (16 in total). It is a **small, anonymised subset** of real
recordings of an acoustic monitoring project:

- **Fictitious device ID** (`FACADE0012345678`): it is not the ID of any
  real recorder.
- **Fictitious location** (`41.00°N 3.00°W`, with the same precision of two
  decimals that AudioMoth writes): it is not the place where the recordings
  were made.
- **Reduced size**: most WAV files were cut to 0.05 s (no useful audio: they
  only show the names and metadata of a real card). **6 of the 16** files
  keep about 7 s with real song, enough for BirdNET to detect something.
- Since the cut files last less than 3 s, 10 of the 16 recordings appear as
  `problem: "duration < 3 s"` in the inventory below. **This is on
  purpose**: it also shows how `read_audiomoth()` flags faulty recordings of
  a real card.

```{r}
library(AudiomothR)

example_card <- system.file("extdata", "example", "card", package = "AudiomothR")
example_card
```

## 1. Reading the card: `CONFIG.TXT`, location and inventory

`read_audiomoth()` takes the root folder of the card (the one that contains
`CONFIG.TXT` and the daily folders); without a folder, `choose_folder()` opens
a dialog. AudioMoth only writes the location in `CONFIG.TXT` when it was set
in its configuration app, and with two decimals (about 700 m), so giving the
coordinates of the site is recommended. `coordinates` accepts the text copied
from Google Earth or Google Maps (decimal degrees, degrees-minutes-seconds,
hemisphere letters before or after the numbers, a KML placemark or a Google
Maps link); see `?parse_coordinates`.

The results are saved in the `output` folder. When it is not given,
`read_audiomoth()` asks for it in the console, suggesting a folder in
`~/AudiomothR_results/` (or the one chosen last time for the same box); in
scripts run with `Rscript` it must be given. Here a temporary folder is used,
which disappears when R is closed: **in real use, choose a folder of your
own, outside the card, for each box**. The folder gathers all the cards of
the box: when the SD card is replaced, the next card is read with the same
`output` and its recordings are added as a new *deployment*, with its own
location (the box may have been moved). Reading a card again is fast: the
metadata of the WAV files are kept in a cache in that folder.

```{r}
output <- file.path(tempdir(), "audiomothr_vignette")

am <- read_audiomoth(
  example_card,
  coordinates = "41.00, -3.00",      # fictitious coordinates of the example
  site = "Fictitious example site",
  output = output
)
```

```{r}
am$recordings[, c("file", "start_local", "duration_s", "battery_v", "valid", "problem")]
```

The inventory has, for each recording, the day, the start time in UTC and in
local time (by default `Europe/Madrid`, with daylight saving time), the
duration, the sample rate, the battery voltage, the temperature and the
problems found (unreadable files, interrupted recordings, recordings shorter
than 3 s, without date or duplicated). Recordings triggered by an amplitude
or frequency threshold (`*T.WAV`) are recognised and their silences are
restored before the analysis.

### Copying the card first (recommended)

`read_audiomoth()` never writes on the card, but by default it reads the
recordings **where they are**: the inventory keeps the path of each WAV file
on the card, and the steps that go back to the audio (the examples, the
validation page, a new analysis with other parameters) need the card to be
connected at the same path. Usually, however, the card is formatted and goes
back to the field, and a backup of the recordings is wanted anyway.

With **`copy_to`**, the card is first copied to the disk and everything is
done with the copy:

| `copy_to` | Where the copy goes |
|---|---|
| `NULL` (default) | No copy: the card is read where it is. |
| `TRUE` | Into the results folder: `<output>/recordings/<first date>-<last date>/`. |
| `"/path/to/backup"` | Into a backup folder (e.g. an external disk), one subfolder per box: `/path/to/backup/AudioMoth_<ID>/<first date>-<last date>/`. |

The copy keeps the structure of the card (`CONFIG.TXT` and daily folders) and
the dates of the files, and checks the size of each file. If it is
interrupted (or a file is missing), running it again copies only what is
missing. When it finishes, the card can be formatted (after checking the
copy, as usual). The inventory points to the copy, the original folder of the
card is kept in the column `card_folder` of `am$deployments`, and reading the
copy again later only needs `folder` (no `copy_to`).

```{r}
am_copy <- read_audiomoth(
  example_card,
  coordinates = "41.00, -3.00",
  output = file.path(tempdir(), "audiomothr_vignette_copy"),
  copy_to = TRUE                     # copy into <output>/recordings/
)
am_copy$folder                       # the copy, used from now on
list.files(am_copy$folder)
```

`process_audiomoth()` accepts the same `copy_to` argument.

## 2. Preparing the audio for BirdNET

`prepare_audio()` converts to 48 kHz mono whatever needs it (nothing here:
the AudioMoth already recorded at 48 kHz) and leaves out the recordings with
a `problem`. This step is optional: `analyze_birdnet()` does it by itself.

```{r}
am <- prepare_audio(am)
sum(!is.na(am$recordings$birdnet_path))
```

## 3. Analysing with BirdNET

```{r, eval = FALSE}
setup_birdnet()             # optional: installs Python, TensorFlow and the model beforehand
am <- analyze_birdnet(am)   # the first time it installs them if setup_birdnet() was not run
```

This adds `am$detections` and saves `AudioMoth_<ID>_detections.csv` in the
results folder. Each recording is analysed once: if the analysis is
interrupted, running it again continues where it stopped. By default only the
species expected at the site and week of each recording are considered
(location filter of BirdNET, see below), and the common names are in the
language of the operating system (argument `language`, e.g.
`language = "es"`).

### Which species BirdNET looks for

BirdNET v2.4 knows about 6,500 classes, most of them birds of the whole
world. Without any filter it often proposes species of other continents, so
`analyze_birdnet()` offers three options.

**1. The location filter (default).** BirdNET has, besides the model that
listens to the audio, a *metadata* (geographic) model trained with the eBird
checklists. Given a latitude, a longitude and a week of the year (48 weeks,
four per month), it returns for each species a *probability of occurrence*:
roughly, how often the species is reported in eBird checklists around that
place in that week. `analyze_birdnet()` asks for it at the location of each
deployment and for the week of each recording, and only the species with a
probability of at least `location_threshold` (0.03, the value of BirdNET) are
analysed; **the others are never proposed**, whatever the audio. On the
example site, about 156 species pass the filter in October.

The filter removes most of the absurd identifications, but it inherits the
biases of eBird. It may leave out species that **are** present:

- in **little visited areas**, with few eBird checklists;
- **nocturnal or secretive** species, rarely reported in daytime checklists
  (owls such as the long-eared owl, the Eurasian stone-curlew, the nightjars);
- **scarce or local** species (sandgrouse and other steppe birds, scarce
  migrants);
- recordings made **outside the usual season** of the species at the site.

For example, in the steppes of Villafáfila (Zamora, Spain; 41.84°N
5.60°W), in May (weeks 17 and 19 of BirdNET), the filter keeps the Eurasian
stone-curlew (probability 0.042) but leaves out the little bustard (0.028),
the Eurasian scops owl (0.026), the pin-tailed and the black-bellied
sandgrouse (0.010 and 0.009) and the long-eared owl (0.002), all of them
observed within 25 km in spring according to GBIF.

When the aim is precisely to find such species, change the filter:

| Situation | Option |
|---|---|
| Common species, well visited area, records for citizen science | Default filter (`location_threshold = 0.03`) |
| Some expected species are missing | Lower the threshold: `location_threshold = 0.01` |
| Rare, nocturnal or steppe species; little visited areas | Own list of species (`species_list`, option 2) |
| Exploratory analysis, everything is checked by ear | No filter: `location_filter = FALSE` (more mistakes; use `create_validation()`) |

Whatever the option, the probability of occurrence is kept in the column
`location_prob` of the detections, and the validation page shows first the
least plausible records (low confidence and low `location_prob`), so the
species that the model does not expect are the first to be checked by ear.

**2. An own list of species (`species_list`).** Only the species of the list
are analysed, wherever the recorder is; the location filter is then not
applied. The list may be given as:

- a **vector** of scientific names:
  `species_list = c("Burhinus oedicnemus", "Asio otus", "Pterocles orientalis")`;
- the **species list of BirdNET-Analyzer** (a `.txt` file, one species per
  line as `Burhinus oedicnemus_Eurasian Stone-curlew`, or just scientific
  names): lists prepared for the desktop version of BirdNET can be used as
  they are;
- a **CSV file** (or a data frame) with a column of scientific names, named
  `scientific_name` (or `scientific name`, `Scientific Name`, `species`,
  `taxon`...; otherwise the first column is used). Other columns (common
  name, notes...) are ignored. The package includes a template:

```{r}
template <- system.file("extdata", "example", "species_list.csv", package = "AudiomothR")
read.csv(template)
```

The names may follow BirdNET (eBird/Clements), the IOC World Bird List,
Observation.org or GBIF: `read_species_list()` translates them into the
names of BirdNET, keeps all the BirdNET species of a name that another
taxonomy lumps, and reports the names that BirdNET does not know (it cannot
detect them). Use it to check a list before the analysis:

```{r}
read_species_list(c("Burhinus oedicnemus", "Asio otus", "Carduelis chloris"))
```

*Carduelis chloris* (an old name, still a synonym in Observation.org) becomes
*Chloris chloris*. Names that are not found in the tables of the package (e.g.
*Parus caeruleus*) are looked up in GBIF when there is a connection, and those
that BirdNET cannot detect are reported (e.g. *Otis tarda*: BirdNET v2.4 has
no model of the great bustard).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
am <- analyze_birdnet(am, species_list = "~/my_species_list.txt")   # BirdNET-Analyzer
am <- analyze_birdnet(am, species_list = template)                  # CSV file
```

Each list is a different analysis, with its own cache: going back to an
earlier list (or to the location filter) reuses its results.

**3. A list built from GBIF.** A good list of the species *observed* around
the site can be taken from GBIF (<https://www.gbif.org>), which publishes the
observations of eBird, Observation.org and iNaturalist, among many others.
`gbif_species_list()` asks GBIF which bird species have been observed within
`radius_km` of the recorder, in the months of the recordings and in the last
ten years, and translates them into BirdNET names. **No account or key is
needed**, only an internet connection.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Around the deployments of the box, in the months of its recordings
species <- gbif_species_list(am, radius_km = 25, file = "~/species_box_01.csv")
head(species)   # scientific_name, english_name, gbif_name, records (occurrences), match

# Review or edit the CSV (e.g. remove or add species), then use it
am <- analyze_birdnet(am, species_list = "~/species_box_01.csv")

# Or around some coordinates, all the year, with every dataset of GBIF
species <- gbif_species_list("42.34, -3.70", radius_km = 50, months = 1:12, datasets = "all")
```

How wide should the area be? A radius of 25-50 km, or a whole province,
usually gives a list complete enough to include the scarce species without
bringing in those of other regions. In little visited areas use a larger
radius, and with `min_records = 2` or more, species recorded only once
(perhaps by mistake) are left out. The species of GBIF that BirdNET cannot
detect are listed in `attr(species, "not_in_birdnet")`. The data belong to
the observers and the publishers of each dataset: if the list is used in a
publication, cite GBIF and its queries (`attr(species, "queries")`, see
`?gbif_species_list`).

Instead of running it here, we load the detections that `analyze_birdnet()`
returned for this same card, saved in the package:

```{r}
am$detections <- read_detections(
  system.file("extdata", "example", "birdnet_detections.csv", package = "AudiomothR")
)
am$detections[, c("local_time", "start_s", "scientific_name", "confidence", "no_doubts")]
```

BirdNET analyses the 6 valid recordings and returns 6 detections of 4
species, all of them in the recordings of 7 October. In the recording of
08:40, in both 3 s windows BirdNET hesitates between the grey wagtail
(*Motacilla cinerea*) and the white wagtail (*Motacilla alba*):
`no_doubts = FALSE`.

## 4. From detections to a summary by species

```{r}
species_summary(am, min_confidence = 0.5)
```

To choose the species of the examples without typing their names,
`detected_species()` prints a vector ready to copy, change the number of
examples of each species and paste into `extract_examples()`. It also returns
that vector, so it can be passed on directly:

```{r}
species <- detected_species(am, example_confidence = 0.5)
```

## 5. Audio, spectrogram and video examples

`extract_examples()` chooses the best detections of the species (by default
with a confidence of at least 0.85, without doubts and at most one per
recording; here the threshold is lowered to 0.5) and creates, for each one, a
clip of the audio with a margin before and after the detection, its
spectrogram and an MP4 video of the spectrogram with its audio.

```{r, eval = ffmpeg_ok}
extract_examples(am, species, min_confidence = 0.5, margin_s = 0.5)
list.files(file.path(output, "examples"), recursive = TRUE)
```

```{r, eval = !ffmpeg_ok, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("_(This block was not run when building the vignette: ffmpeg was not found on this computer.)_\n")
```

## 6. Validating the records by ear (optional)

BirdNET makes mistakes, above all with species that are unusual at the site
or detected with low confidence, and Observation.org receives whatever is
exported. Before exporting, the records can be checked by ear with
`create_validation()`. It is optional and takes time (a few seconds per
record), but it is the best guarantee against wrong records.

```{r}
page <- create_validation(am, min_confidence = 0.5, open = FALSE)
```

The function writes a folder `validation/` in the results with:

- `AudioMoth_<ID>_validation.html`: a web page that works offline, in any
  browser and **without R** (the folder can be sent to an ornithologist);
- `clips/`: the audio clips (and their spectrograms) of the best detections
  of each record;
- `AudioMoth_<ID>_validation.csv`: the list of records, with empty columns
  `decision` and `new_name`.

The page has **one card per species and day** (the unit of a record of
Observation.org), sorted **from the least plausible to the most plausible**:
first the species with the lowest product of their highest confidence and
their probability of occurrence at the site and week (from the BirdNET
metadata model). For each card it shows the number of detections, the
highest confidence, how expected the species is at the site, the other
species that BirdNET proposed in the same windows, and up to `n_clips` clips
from different recordings. Listen and decide:

| Decision | Keyboard | Effect on `export_observation()` |
|---|---|---|
| **Valid** | `V` | The record is exported, even with a single detection or a confidence below `min_confidence`, with `is certain = True`. |
| **Not valid** | `N` | The record is not exported. |
| **Unsure** | `U` | The usual criteria apply (`min_confidence`, `min_detections`). |
| **Other species** | (type) | The record is exported under the chosen species (with autocompletion among all the BirdNET species). |

`J`/`K` move between cards and `Space` plays the first clip. Decisions are
kept in the browser while working (you can close the page and come back).
When you finish, press **Download decisions (CSV)**: the browser saves
`AudioMoth_<ID>_validation.csv` in the Downloads folder. Instead of the page,
the CSV of the validation folder can also be filled in with a spreadsheet
(columns `decision`: `valid`, `invalid` or `unsure`, and `new_name`).

`read_validation()` finds the decisions (in the validation folder or in the
Downloads folder, the most recent file) and `export_observation()` applies
them automatically. To show it here, we write the file that the page would
download, with two decisions:

```{r}
decisions <- read.csv(file.path(output, "validation", "AudioMoth_FACADE0012345678_validation.csv"))
decisions$decision[decisions$scientific_name == "Troglodytes troglodytes"] <- "valid"
decisions$decision[decisions$scientific_name == "Motacilla cinerea"] <- "invalid"
write.csv(decisions, file.path(output, "validation", "AudioMoth_FACADE0012345678_validation.csv"),
          row.names = FALSE, na = "")
read_validation(am)[, c("date", "scientific_name", "decision", "new_name")]
```

Running `create_validation()` again (e.g. after analysing more recordings)
keeps the decisions already taken.

## 7. Exporting to Observation.org

`export_observation()` turns the detections into the import format of
Observation.org: one record per species and day, by default only with
detections of confidence ≥ 0.80 and at least two detections that day, plus
the records validated by ear. BirdNET names (eBird/Clements taxonomy) are
translated, through the IOC World Bird List v15.2, into the names of the bird
species of Observation.org (which has some lumps and genera of its own);
labels that are not birds (human voice, noise, frogs, insects...) are left
out, and species split by IOC are translated according to the location or
reported.

```{r}
obs <- export_observation(am)
obs[, c("date", "time", "scientific name", "is certain", "notes")]
```

With the default criteria, this card alone would not produce any record: no
species has two detections of at least 0.80 on the same day. The Eurasian
wren appears because it was validated as correct (and the grey wagtail does
not, because it was marked as not valid). Without validation, the criteria
can be relaxed:

```{r}
obs <- export_observation(am, min_confidence = 0.5, min_detections = 1, validation = FALSE)
obs[, c("date", "time", "scientific name", "is certain")]
```

The records that have not been validated are always marked `is certain =
False`: the identification is automatic and BirdNET sometimes fails. If the
CSV is edited by hand, a new export does not overwrite it (it is saved with
the date in its name), and the criteria used are saved next to it in
`AudioMoth_<ID>_observation.json`.

## 8. PDF report

`create_report()` prepares a Quarto folder with everything it needs and
renders a PDF with the summary of the sampling, the map of the recorders, the
state of the recordings (by day, problems, battery and temperature), the
detected species with their confidence and activity by day and by hour, the
spectrograms of the examples, the records for Observation.org and the result
of the validation. It needs Quarto (≥ 1.4; RStudio and Positron already
include it), but not LaTeX.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
create_report(am)                                     # one recorder

# Several recorders: one section each (by_recorder = TRUE) or all together
create_report(list(am1, am2, am3), by_recorder = FALSE, output = "report_river")
```

The map is drawn on OpenStreetMap when `maptiles`, `sf` and `terra` are
installed and there is an Internet connection; otherwise only the points are
shown. The report folder can be edited (`report.qmd`) and rendered again with
`quarto render report.qmd`; `create_report()` keeps those edits.

## Everything in one call: `process_audiomoth()`

```{r, eval = FALSE}
am <- process_audiomoth(
  folder = example_card,
  coordinates = "41.00, -3.00",
  output = "~/AudiomothR_results/example_box",
  copy_to = TRUE,                    # copy of the card in <output>/recordings/
  example_species = "auto",          # the species proposed by detected_species()
  example_confidence = 0.5,
  validation = TRUE,                 # creates the validation page
  report = TRUE                      # creates the PDF report
)
```

It chains steps 1 to 8 (it needs the real BirdNET, so it is not run here).
`example_species` also accepts the vector printed by `detected_species()`,
and the arguments of `analyze_birdnet()` can be added, e.g.
`species_list = "~/my_species_list.txt"`.
Observation.org is exported with the default criteria only the first time
(`export = TRUE` exports again); after validating the records, call
`export_observation(am)` to apply the decisions.

See `?process_audiomoth` and the `README.md` of the package for more details
on each function.
